clinicalPearls: The commonest cause of a persistent head tilt in infancy, arising from fibrosis and shortening of the sternocleidomastoid muscle
The head tilts toward the affected side while the chin rotates to the opposite side, the characteristic posture produced by unilateral sternocleidomastoid tightness
In early infancy a firm, non-tender sternocleidomastoid tumour, an olive-like swelling within the muscle belly, may be palpable and typically regresses over the following months
Positional (deformational) plagiocephaly and facial asymmetry commonly accompany the tilt because the infant consistently rests the head in one position
There is a well-recognised association with developmental dysplasia of the hip and with other packaging deformities, so the hips must always be examined
Early passive stretching physiotherapy, along with positioning and handling advice, resolves the great majority of cases when begun in the first months of life
Deformity that persists beyond about one year despite stretching may require surgical release of the sternocleidomastoid
reference.pathophysiology: Congenital muscular torticollis results from localised fibrosis and shortening of the sternocleidomastoid, thought to follow a compartment-like injury or ischaemia of the muscle related to intrauterine position or a difficult, often breech, delivery. Fibrous tissue replaces part of the muscle, sometimes forming a palpable tumour early on, and the resulting contracture tethers the head into tilt toward the affected side and rotation away from it. Because the deforming posture is constant, the growing skull and face remodel asymmetrically, producing plagiocephaly and hemifacial flattening. The same intrauterine crowding that injures the muscle is thought to underlie the association with developmental hip dysplasia and other moulding deformities.
additionalDifferentials: Bony torticollis from Klippel-Feil syndrome or other cervical vertebral anomaly
Atlantoaxial rotatory subluxation or other cervical instability
Ocular torticollis from strabismus or a cranial nerve palsy
Neurological causes such as a posterior fossa tumour or Chiari malformation
Sandifer syndrome associated with gastro-oesophageal reflux
Inflammatory or infective causes such as cervical lymphadenitis or a retropharyngeal abscess
additionalInvestigations: Clinical examination of neck range of movement and palpation of the sternocleidomastoid
Examination of the hips, with ultrasound for developmental dysplasia where indicated
Ultrasound of the sternocleidomastoid to confirm fibrosis when the diagnosis is uncertain
Cervical spine radiographs when a bony anomaly or instability is suspected
Ophthalmological assessment if an ocular cause is considered
Neuroimaging if neurological signs or an atypical presentation raise concern for a central cause
redFlags: Absence of a tight sternocleidomastoid, or a tilt that does not fit a muscular pattern, suggesting a bony, ocular, or neurological cause
Neurological signs, or torticollis of later or sudden onset
Failure to improve with, or worsening despite, appropriate stretching physiotherapy
Associated developmental dysplasia of the hip
Progressive facial asymmetry or severe fixed contracture
reference.prognosis: The outlook is excellent when treatment begins early, as most infants achieve full correction with stretching and positioning; later presentation or a persistent tight band carries a greater chance of residual deformity and a need for surgical release.
pitfalls: Assuming every infantile head tilt is muscular and missing a bony, ocular, or neurological cause
Failing to examine the hips and overlooking coexisting dysplasia
Delaying stretching physiotherapy, which is most effective in the early months
Neglecting positioning advice, allowing plagiocephaly and facial asymmetry to worsen
Persisting with conservative treatment indefinitely when surgical release is indicated
management: First-line passive sternocleidomastoid stretching physiotherapy begun early in infancy
Positioning and handling advice encouraging rotation toward the restricted side and reducing the sustained deforming posture
Repositioning, tummy-time and, where needed, cranial remoulding orthosis to address positional plagiocephaly and facial asymmetry
Always examine and screen the hips for associated developmental dysplasia
Surgical sternocleidomastoid release reserved for a persistent tight band or late presentation failing conservative care
Follow-up to monitor neck range of movement, facial symmetry and correction through growth
